\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can give both object pronoun sets and say which row is the only one where they differ in shape.}

Complete ES-C46-repaso-dos-sistemas: give the six indirect pronouns and count the distinct shapes across both tables.

\section[Practice]{Review — two systems, two new words}

\label{lesson:ES-C46-repaso-dos-sistemas}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new. Two questions before the tables: where does an object pronoun go, and what single question chooses between the two sets?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{direct — \emph{what}} & \textbf{indirect — \emph{to whom}} \\
\midrule
me & \textbf{me} & \textbf{me} \\
you & \textbf{te} & \textbf{te} \\
him / her / usted & \textbf{lo}, \textbf{la} & \textbf{le} \\
us & \textbf{nos} & \textbf{nos} \\
you all \emph{(Spain)} & \textbf{os} & \textbf{os} \\
them / ustedes & \textbf{los}, \textbf{las} & \textbf{les} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Twelve cells. \textbf{Two of them are new since the last review}, and you produced one of those yourself by adding an \emph{-s}.

Do the arithmetic once and it will stay done. Fourteen chapters of object pronouns have asked you to learn, as shapes: \emph{te}, \emph{lo}, \emph{la}, \emph{nos}, \emph{os}, \emph{le}. Six words. \emph{Me} you had from chapter four; \emph{los}, \emph{las} and \emph{les} you derived. Six words, spread across fourteen chapters, with a review and a synthesis at each joint — that is what a gentle ramp costs and what it buys.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the one asymmetry}]
Read the third row again, because it is the only place the two columns disagree in shape rather than spelling:

\begin{quote}
direct: \textbf{lo} / \textbf{la} — two forms, gender marked. indirect: \textbf{le} — one form, gender not marked.
\end{quote}

Spanish cares about the gender of a thing being acted on and does not care about the gender of a person being aimed at. There is no deep reason for it; Latin's dative simply had one form where its accusative had two, and Spanish inherited the asymmetry whole.

It is good news. The row that carries all the difficulty in one column carries none in the other.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the direct six, then the indirect six, and hear how much is the same
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lo tengo, le hablo, los tengo, les hablo\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until the shared four stop feeling like two separate lists.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many pronouns are shared between the two sets? (\textbf{Four}.) Which row differs? (\textbf{Him / her / usted} — \emph{lo} and \emph{la} against \emph{le}.) Next: both sets in one conversation, where you have to choose fast.
\end{tcolorbox}
